source.title: On Anger
source.attribution: Seneca, On Anger (trans. Aubrey Stewart), Standard Ebooks, public domain
source.notes: Taken from Seneca, Dialogues (trans. Aubrey Stewart), Standard Ebooks.

cards.title: Delay is the strongest cure for anger
cards.body:
Seneca's top remedy is not suppressing anger but postponing it. Ask your anger for time, not to forgive the offence, but to judge it properly. The first surge is fierce; given a pause, it often fades by itself.

This is the logic behind sleeping on an angry email or stepping out before replying in an argument. You lose nothing by waiting. If the complaint is valid, it will still be valid in an hour, and you'll express it better.
cards.quote: The greatest remedy for anger is delay: beg anger to grant you this at the first, not in order that it may pardon the offence, but that it may form a right judgment about it
cards.apply_it: Set a personal rule for today: no reply to anything that angers you for at least an hour. Draft it if you must, but don't send.

quiz.question: Why did Seneca recommend delaying anger?
options: Because anger is always justified later
To make the other person wait
So you can form a right judgement about the offence
quiz.explanation: Delay lets the first fierce impulse pass so judgement can take over.

cards.title: Suspicion always finds evidence, so choose a kinder reading
cards.body:
Seneca lists small slights we take personally: someone greeted us coldly, cut short our story, didn't invite us. Suspicion will never run short of proof, he warns. Look for an insult and you will find one.

What helps is straightforwardness and a generous interpretation. A colleague's short reply may mean they're swamped; a friend's silence may mean they're struggling. Believe the worst only when it's unmistakable, and notice how often your suspicions turn out wrong.
cards.quote: Suspicion will never lack grounds: what we want is straightforwardness, and a kindly interpretation of things.
cards.apply_it: When someone's behaviour bothers you today, list two innocent explanations before settling on the unkind one.

quiz.question: What did Seneca recommend instead of suspicion?
quiz.explanation: Because suspicion always finds grounds, he urged a kind reading of others' actions.

cards.title: Before blaming someone, ask whether you have done the same thing
cards.body:
Seneca noticed that we judge the act and ignore the person behind it. Rarely do we ask: have I ever done this? Was it on purpose or an accident? Were they under pressure, mistaken, or trying to help someone else?

Asking those questions turns a flash of anger into understanding. The late colleague, the forgetful partner, the driver who cut you off: you have probably been each of them at some point. Putting yourself in their place makes fairness much easier.
cards.quote: No one says to himself, “I myself have done or might have done this very thing which I am angry with another for doing.” No one considers the intention of the doer, but merely the thing done
cards.apply_it: Next time someone annoys you, quietly ask yourself: when did I last do something similar, and why?

quiz.question: What question did Seneca say we rarely ask ourselves when angry with others?
options: "Have I myself done or might I do this same thing?"
quiz.explanation: Recognising our own similar faults, and the doer's intention, softens anger.

cards.title: Most of what makes us furious is trivial
cards.body:
Seneca catalogues the triggers of anger: a careless word, a slow servant, a disrespectful gesture, a remark taken the wrong way. Look closely, he says, and they are the sort of things children squabble over. What fuels our rage is giving huge value to small matters.

The parking spot, the reply-all, the dishes left in the sink. Asking "Will this matter in a week?" often deflates the anger on the spot and frees energy for things that do matter.
cards.quote: the things which cause us such great heat are trifles, the sort of things that children fight and squabble over: there is nothing serious, nothing important in all that we do with such gloomy faces. It is, I repeat, the setting a great value on trifles that is the cause of your anger and madness.
cards.apply_it: The next time you feel irritated today, ask: will this matter in a week? If not, let it pass.

quiz.question: According to Seneca, what lies behind most of our anger?
options: Setting a great value on trifles
quiz.explanation: He wrote that putting high value on trifles is the cause of anger.

cards.title: End each day with a short, honest review of yourself
cards.body:
Seneca admired the philosopher Sextius, who asked himself every night: what bad habit did I cure today? What fault did I resist? How am I better? Seneca believed anger softens when it knows it will be called up for review each evening.

It's a gentle form of accountability, not self-punishment. A few minutes of reflection turns vague intentions into feedback, and he noted that sleep after such a review is especially peaceful.
cards.quote: It was the custom of Sextius when the day was over, and he had betaken himself to rest, to inquire of his spirit: “What bad habit of yours have you cured today? what vice have you checked? in what respect are you better?”
cards.apply_it: Tonight before sleep, answer Sextius's three questions in a sentence each. Repeat for a week.

quiz.question: Why did Seneca think a nightly self-examination helps with anger?
options: It helps you forget what happened
Anger softens when it knows it will be reviewed daily
quiz.explanation: Knowing it must face daily review makes anger more restrained.

cards.title: Life is short: spend it practising kindness, not feuding
cards.body:
Seneca closes his long study of anger with a reminder of mortality. The breath we hold dear will soon leave us. While we're still among people, he says, let's be humane and not a source of fear or harm to anyone.

Grudges and long fights assume we have endless time to waste. We don't. Remembering that every relationship is temporary makes it easier to let small wrongs go and to choose warmth with the people around us now.
cards.quote: This breath that we hold so dear will soon leave us: in the meantime, while we draw it, while we live among human beings, let us practise humanity: let us not be a terror or a danger to anyone.
cards.apply_it: Think of a grudge you're holding. Ask whether it's worth keeping given how short time is, and take one step to ease it.

quiz.question: What did Seneca urge us to practise while we live among others?
quiz.explanation: Because life is brief, he urged us to practise humanity and harm no one.

cards.title: Treat anger as a brief madness, not as a reliable guide
cards.body:
Seneca opens his book by agreeing with older thinkers who called anger a temporary insanity. While it lasts, it ignores advice, forgets family ties, and cannot see what is fair. Worse, it often wrecks the angry person along with the target, like a boulder that shatters on whatever it lands on.

Thinking of anger this way is useful. You wouldn't sign a contract or make a big promise while delirious, so don't make big decisions while furious either. Notice the state, name it, and wait until you're yourself again.
cards.quote: Some of the wisest of men have in consequence of this called anger a short madness
cards.apply_it: Next time you feel anger rising, say to yourself: 'I'm temporarily not myself.' Postpone any decision until that passes.

quiz.question: Why did Seneca compare anger to a falling rock?
options: It is slow to start moving
It can be easily stopped once in motion
It only harms the person it lands on
It breaks itself on whatever it crushes
quiz.explanation: Anger damages the angry person as well as the target, like a rock that shatters on impact.

cards.title: Stop anger at the border, before it takes over the mind
cards.body:
Seneca argues it is far easier to keep anger out than to control it once it is inside. When a passion takes hold, it doesn't sit beside your reason waiting for orders; your mind itself turns into the passion. From then on, it does as much as it likes, not as much as you allow.

So the moment to act is the very first spark: the irritated thought, the tight jaw, the urge to fire back. That's when a pause, a breath or a change of scene still works. Ten minutes later, you may no longer be in charge.
cards.quote: The enemy, I repeat, must be met and driven back at the outermost frontier-line
cards.apply_it: List three early signs that you're getting angry (a phrase you use, a feeling in your body). When one shows up, step away for five minutes.

quiz.question: According to Seneca, when is the best time to deal with anger?
options: Only once the other person apologises
quiz.explanation: Once anger enters the mind it takes over reason, so it must be resisted at the outset.

cards.title: You don't need anger to have energy or drive
cards.body:
Some people defend anger as fuel: a little of it, they say, makes you braver and more determined. Seneca disagrees. If anger obeys reason, it isn't really anger; if it doesn't obey, it's a danger. Either way, reason can do the job alone, and a mild dose of a harmful thing is still harmful, just less so.

The same applies at work or in sport. Firmness, focus and persistence come from deciding something matters, not from being furious. Anger tends to make your effort sloppy and short-lived.
cards.quote: wherefore a moderate passion is nothing but a moderate evil
cards.apply_it: Think of a goal you push towards with frustration. Write one calm reason it matters to you, and use that as your motivation instead.

quiz.question: What did Seneca say about keeping anger 'in moderation'?
options: Moderate anger is the key to success
A moderate passion is just a moderate evil
Anger is only harmful in large amounts
quiz.explanation: Seneca held that reducing a harmful passion only reduces the harm; it doesn't make it good.

cards.title: Correct people when you're calm, never in the heat of anger
cards.body:
Seneca tells how Socrates once said to a servant who had done wrong that he would punish him if he weren't angry. Socrates postponed the correction until he was calm, and dealt with himself first.

Seneca's point is that correction is meant to help someone improve, and that works far better when it comes from steady judgement than from rage. If even Socrates didn't trust himself while angry, the rest of us shouldn't either. Whether you're a parent, manager or teacher, wait until you can correct without the heat.
cards.quote: This is why Socrates said to the slave, “I would strike you, were I not angry.” He put off the correction of the slave to a calmer season; at the moment, he corrected himself.
cards.apply_it: If someone at home or work needs correcting today and you feel angry, say 'Let's talk about this later' and set a time when you'll be calm.

quiz.question: What did Socrates do when he was angry with a servant?
options: Punished him immediately to set an example
Postponed the correction until he was calm
quiz.explanation: Socrates corrected himself first and left the correction for a calmer moment.

cards.title: If they're weaker, spare them; if they're stronger, spare yourself
cards.body:
Seneca offers a neat rule for when someone hurts you. Whoever offended you is either weaker or stronger than you. If they're weaker, revenge is beneath you and simply cruel. If they're stronger, revenge is dangerous and will likely cost you more than the original hurt.

He adds that revenge is really an admission that you've been wounded, while a strong mind lets insults bounce off like weapons off armour. Before hitting back at a colleague, relative or rival, ask which category they fall into. In both cases, restraint usually wins.
cards.quote: He who has hurt you must be either stronger or weaker than yourself. If he be weaker, spare him: if he be stronger, spare yourself.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone you want to get back at. Are they weaker or stronger than you? Write down what revenge would actually cost you.

quiz.question: What is Seneca's advice if the person who hurt you is stronger than you?
options: Strike first before they strike again
Pretend to be friends, then get revenge
quiz.explanation: Against the stronger, revenge is risky; Seneca advises sparing yourself.

cards.title: Anger would rather stay wrong than admit a mistake
cards.body:
Seneca describes a Roman commander, Piso, who ordered a soldier executed for supposedly murdering his comrade. When the 'murdered' comrade turned up alive, Piso, now furious, had both men killed, plus the officer who had stopped the execution. Anger invented three crimes because it could find none.

The lesson is uncomfortable: when angry, we would rather double down than say 'I was wrong'. We find new reasons to justify the position we took. If you notice yourself defending a decision more fiercely the more evidence piles up against it, anger or pride may be steering.
cards.quote: It hates to be proved wrong, and thinks it more honourable to persevere in a mistaken line of conduct than to retract it.
cards.apply_it: Recall a recent argument where you dug in. Is there a part you can now admit was wrong? Tell the person.

quiz.question: In Seneca's story, what did Piso do when the 'murdered' soldier appeared alive?
options: Ordered both soldiers and the officer executed
Promoted the officer for his good sense
Held a fair trial to examine the evidence
quiz.explanation: Anger refused to admit its error and invented new reasons to punish.

cards.title: Anger wastes time and opportunity on battles that don't matter
cards.body:
Seneca tells of the Persian king Cyrus, marching to attack Babylon. When a river swept away one of his prized horses, he flew into a rage and set his whole army to dig channels until the river was split into hundreds of streams. He won his war against the river, but lost precious time, his soldiers' spirit, and the chance to surprise his real enemy.

In work and life we do the same: we pour energy into getting even with a minor obstacle or person and forget the actual goal. Anger narrows vision to the insult in front of us.
cards.quote: Thus he lost time, which is very important in great operations, and lost, also, the soldiers’ courage, which was broken by useless labour
cards.apply_it: Ask yourself: is there a 'river' you're fighting right now, a petty grudge eating time you need for a bigger goal? Drop it this week.

quiz.question: What did Cyrus lose by punishing the river?
options: Time, his soldiers' courage and the element of surprise
Nothing; it made his army stronger
quiz.explanation: His anger diverted the army from its real goal, costing time, morale and opportunity.

cards.title: Master your anger before you try to master the situation
cards.body:
Seneca praises the Roman general Fabius, who faced Hannibal when Rome was close to collapse. Instead of charging in to avenge earlier defeats, Fabius counted his limited forces, set aside grief and revenge, and played a long, patient game. Seneca's verdict: he beat his own anger first, and that is how he beat Hannibal.

In a crisis, the temptation is to react hard and fast to show strength. But the people who come through are usually the ones who keep a cool head, take stock and wait for the right moment.
cards.quote: he laid aside thoughts of grief and revenge, turning his sole attention to what was profitable and to making the most of his opportunities, and conquered his anger before he conquered Hannibal.
cards.apply_it: Facing a setback? Before acting, write down your resources and the one move that helps most, ignoring what would merely feel satisfying.

quiz.question: According to Seneca, what did Fabius conquer before Hannibal?
quiz.explanation: Fabius set aside revenge and grief, which allowed him to wait patiently and win.

cards.title: Leading by fear makes you afraid too
cards.body:
Some defend anger because it makes people fear you. Seneca replies that being feared is a poor goal: it makes you hated, and hatred is more dangerous than being looked down on. He quotes a line that caught the Roman public's mood during civil war, warning that whoever many fear must in turn fear many.

A boss, parent or leader who rules by outbursts ends up surrounded by resentment and quiet resistance, always watching their back. Respect earned through fairness and calm lasts longer and lets you sleep at night.
cards.quote: “He must fear many, whom so many fear.”
cards.apply_it: Think of a leader you admire. Do people follow them out of fear or respect? Pick one habit of theirs to copy this week.

quiz.question: Why did Seneca reject using anger to make others fear you?
options: Fear is the most reliable way to lead
Anger is too tiring to keep up
Whoever is feared by many must fear many in turn
quiz.explanation: Inspiring terror makes you hated, and whatever terrifies others lives in fear itself.

cards.title: The first jolt isn't anger yet; anger is what you choose next
cards.body:
Seneca separates three stages. First comes an involuntary jolt when you feel wronged: a flush, a start, a racing heart. You can't prevent it any more than you can stop blinking. Next comes a thought: 'I've been wronged, they should pay.' Finally, if you agree with that thought, anger takes over and wants revenge regardless of whether it's right.

This is freeing. Feeling the jolt doesn't make you an angry person, and it isn't a failure. The real choice comes in the second stage, when you can question the story you're telling yourself.
cards.quote: learn that the first emotion is involuntary, and is, as it were, a preparation for a passion, and a threatening of one.
cards.apply_it: Next time you feel the jolt, notice it without judging, then ask: 'What story am I about to believe?' Question that story before you act.

quiz.question: According to Seneca, what is the first stage of anger?
options: An involuntary jolt you can't prevent
A deliberate decision to get revenge
A calm judgement of the facts
quiz.explanation: The first emotion is involuntary; anger proper begins when the mind agrees to seek revenge.

cards.title: To stop being angry at people, forgive them for being human
cards.body:
If you get angry every time someone is careless, rude or foolish, Seneca warns, you will be angry all day. Mistakes are not rare exceptions; they are part of being human. We are angry with grown-ups for things we would excuse in children, though being human is an even better excuse than being young.

Seneca's solution is to forgive the whole human race in advance. That isn't approving of bad behaviour; it's accepting that people will fall short, including you, so each new failing doesn't come as a shock.
cards.quote: To avoid being angry with individuals, you must pardon the whole mass, you must grant forgiveness to the entire human race.
cards.apply_it: Write down the mistake that most often irritates you in others. Then write one time you made the same kind of mistake.

quiz.question: What does Seneca suggest to avoid being angry with individuals?
options: Only spend time with wise people
quiz.explanation: Since everyone errs, forgiving humanity as a whole frees you from constant anger at individuals.

cards.title: Start the day expecting difficult people, and treat them like a doctor would
cards.body:
Seneca suggests a morning mindset for the wise person: today I'll meet people who are greedy, ungrateful, drunk or obsessed with status. Not as a gloomy prediction, but so none of it comes as a surprise. Then deal with them as a doctor deals with patients, aiming to help, not to rage.

He compares it to a leaking ship. The sailor doesn't scream at the sea or the planks; he bails water and plugs holes, knowing the job never fully ends. Expecting trouble keeps you calm enough to handle it.
cards.quote: “Many men will meet me who are drunkards, lustful, ungrateful, greedy, and excited by the frenzy of ambition.” He will view all these as benignly as a physician does his patients.
cards.apply_it: Tomorrow morning, take ten seconds to tell yourself: 'Someone will annoy me today. I'll respond like a doctor, not a fighter.'

quiz.question: How does Seneca say the wise man views difficult people?
options: As kindly as a physician views his patients
As proof that the world is hopeless
quiz.explanation: He expects their faults and responds with the calm helpfulness of a doctor.

cards.title: Be firm without being furious
cards.body:
Seneca accepts that some situations call for strong, quick action. His advice is to bring force, not anger. He notes that a good speaker may act angry to move an audience, just as an actor plays a part, but the real passion would only cloud his judgement. The goal is to be neither a bully nor a pushover.

In practice, you can set a clear boundary, say no, or demand that something change, all in a steady voice. Firmness keeps you in control; fury hands control to the moment.
cards.quote: Let the wise man be moderate, and when things have to be done somewhat briskly, let him call force, not anger, to his aid.
cards.apply_it: Think of a boundary you need to set. Write the exact sentence you'll use, and practise saying it calmly out loud.

quiz.question: When strong action is needed, what does Seneca say to call on?
quiz.explanation: Firm action can be taken with calm force; anger is not needed.

cards.title: Don't let children win anything by throwing a tantrum
cards.body:
Seneca thought a calm temper is built in childhood. Children who are never refused anything, he warned, can't cope with a 'no' later. He advised that a child should gain nothing by flying into a rage, and should be given, once calm, what was refused while crying. Praise should encourage, but flattery should be kept away.

The principle still holds: if shouting gets results, shouting becomes a habit. Rewarding calm requests teaches children that patience works, a lesson that serves them for life.
cards.quote: Let him obtain nothing by flying into a passion: let him be given when he is quiet what was refused him when he cried for it
cards.apply_it: Next time a child demands something angrily, calmly say: 'Ask me again in a normal voice.' Respond once they do.

quiz.question: What did Seneca advise when a child cries for something?
options: Give it later when they are calm, not while they rage
Give it immediately to stop the crying
Never give it to them at all
quiz.explanation: Children should learn that tantrums gain nothing, while calm requests are heard.

cards.title: Children copy the temper they see at home
cards.body:
Seneca recalls a boy raised in the philosopher Plato's household who went home and saw his father shouting with rage. The boy said he had never seen anyone behave like that at Plato's house. Seneca adds wryly that the boy probably learned to copy his father faster than he had copied Plato.

Young people absorb the habits of the adults closest to them. If you want calm children, students or junior colleagues, your own behaviour under pressure is the lesson they actually learn, far more than any lecture.
cards.quote: “I never saw anyone at Plato’s house act like that.”
cards.apply_it: Next time you're frustrated in front of a child or junior colleague, remember you're giving a lesson. Show them how to handle it calmly.

quiz.question: What was the point of Seneca's story about the boy from Plato's house?
options: Young people imitate the tempers of those around them
quiz.explanation: The boy was shocked by his father's rage, showing how much children absorb from their surroundings.

cards.title: Too much comfort makes small annoyances feel unbearable
cards.body:
Seneca mocks a rich man from Sybaris who complained that watching a labourer dig made him tired, and who suffered because the rose petals on his bed were folded. When life is very soft, he says, the problem isn't that things are hard but that we have become fragile.

The more pampered we are, the more trivial things anger us: a slow waiter, lukewarm tea, a noisy neighbour. Choosing some small discomforts, like cold water, walking instead of riding, or waiting without your phone, can widen your tolerance and shrink your irritations.
cards.quote: When pleasures have corrupted both the body and the mind, nothing seems endurable, not indeed because it is hard, but because he who has to bear it is soft
cards.apply_it: Choose one small comfort to skip today, such as the lift, extra sugar or your phone while waiting, and notice how it feels.

quiz.question: Why, according to Seneca, do pampered people find small things unbearable?
options: Because small things really are the hardest
Because they are smarter than others
Because they have become soft, not because things are hard
Because they work harder than others
quiz.explanation: Luxury makes people fragile, so even trivial discomforts feel intolerable.

cards.title: It isn't a wrong unless it was done on purpose
cards.body:
Seneca points out how often we get angry at things that cannot intend anything: a book with tiny print, a stubborn animal, a broken tool. These can hurt us, the way a stone can, but they cannot wrong us, because a wrong requires intention.

The same test applies to people. A child, someone who didn't know better, or a person who acted by accident caused harm, but didn't mean to insult you. Separating 'this hurt' from 'this was aimed at me' takes much of the heat out of daily frustrations.
cards.quote: we cannot call anything a wrong unless it be done intentionally.
cards.apply_it: When something frustrates you today, ask: 'Did anyone intend this?' If not, deal with the problem without blaming anyone.

quiz.question: Why does Seneca say it is foolish to be angry with objects and animals?
options: They are too small to matter
They will be punished by the gods
They cannot form an intention, so cannot wrong us
quiz.explanation: A wrong requires intention; things and animals can hurt us but cannot wrong us.

cards.title: If a good person hurt you, doubt it; if a bad one did, don't be surprised
cards.body:
Seneca gives a simple two-way test. If someone you know to be good seems to have wronged you, don't believe it too quickly; there's probably a misunderstanding. If someone you know to be dishonest has wronged you, why be shocked? They acted as they always do, and their behaviour will catch up with them.

Either way, outrage isn't the right response. With good people, look for the misunderstanding. With bad ones, adjust your expectations and protect yourself next time, without wasting your peace on surprise.
cards.quote: Is it a good man who has wronged you? do not believe it: is it a bad one? do not be surprised at this
cards.apply_it: Think of a recent hurt. Was it from someone usually good? Ask them about it. From someone unreliable? Change how much you rely on them.

quiz.question: How should you react if a good person seems to have wronged you, according to Seneca?
quiz.explanation: Seneca says to doubt that a good person meant harm, and not to be surprised when a bad one does.

cards.title: Don't condemn a friend on secret, secondhand reports
cards.body:
If you were judging a court case about even a small sum of money, Seneca says, you'd want witnesses, both sides heard, and time to weigh things. Yet we condemn friends on a whisper from someone who refuses to be named or to repeat the claim openly.

Gossip often comes from people who enjoy stirring trouble, want to win your favour, or are themselves mistaken. Before you act on what 'someone told you', go to the person concerned and hear their side. Anyone who will only speak in secret hardly deserves your belief.
cards.quote: The man who will tell you nothing save in secret hardly tells you anything at all. What can be more unjust than to believe in secret, and to be angry openly?
cards.apply_it: If you've heard something negative about someone secondhand, ask them directly and kindly before forming a view.

quiz.question: What does Seneca find most unjust about acting on secret accusations?
options: Asking the accused for their side
Believing in secret but being angry openly
Taking time to check the facts
quiz.explanation: We'd demand evidence in a court case, yet condemn friends on whispers we never test.

cards.title: Most of what enrages us are insults, not real harm
cards.body:
Seneca observes that an angry person quarrels endlessly: with servants, parents, children, strangers. There is always a new irritant, and the anger never leaves. He asks a piercing question: with all this fighting, when will you have time to love?

He also notes that most of what sets us off is a slight to our pride rather than actual damage. Someone being rude, not giving what we hoped for, or delaying our plans isn't the same as robbing or injuring us. Sorting insults from injuries frees time for friendship and real work.
cards.quote: Tell me, miserable man, what time you will have for loving? O, what good time you are wasting on an evil thing!
cards.apply_it: List the last three things that angered you. Mark each 'insult' or 'real harm'. Let the insults go.

quiz.question: What question does Seneca put to the person who is always angry?
options: Who will pay for the damage?
What time will you have for loving?
quiz.explanation: Constant anger uses up the time we could spend on love and friendship.

cards.title: Don't go looking for what people say about you
cards.body:
Seneca's advice for a calmer life is surprisingly simple: don't be nosy. Whoever hunts down every remark made behind their back, digging up spiteful stories even when told in private, destroys their own peace of mind. Many slights pass by harmlessly if you never hear them.

Today that might mean not searching your name online, not asking friends what someone said about you, or not scrolling through comments. Of the remarks that do reach you, Seneca says, ignore some, laugh at others and forgive the rest.
cards.quote: Would you not be irascible? then be not inquisitive.
cards.apply_it: This week, resist checking what others are saying about you, whether online, in group chats or via friends. Notice whether you feel calmer.

quiz.question: What does Seneca say about seeking out what others say about you?
options: It helps you defend your reputation
It is the duty of a wise man
It destroys your own peace of mind
quiz.explanation: Digging up gossip about yourself only gives you more reasons to be angry.

cards.title: 'I didn't expect it' is a poor excuse; expect setbacks
cards.body:
Seneca says we're most enraged by what we didn't see coming, and we tend to treat the unexpected as an injustice. He quotes the Roman general Fabius, who called 'I did not think' the most shameful excuse a commander could make.

People will sometimes be ungrateful, friends will quarrel, children will go wrong. This isn't pessimism; it's realism. Like a sailor who keeps the gear ready to shorten sail even in good weather, expecting some trouble means it doesn't knock you over when it arrives.
cards.quote: Think of everything, expect everything: even with men of good character something queer will crop up
cards.apply_it: Before an important event this week, list two things that could go wrong and how you'd respond calmly to each.

quiz.question: Which excuse did Fabius consider the most shameful?
quiz.explanation: Failing to anticipate trouble is avoidable; expecting it helps us stay calm.

cards.title: Not every insult deserves a reply
cards.body:
A stranger once struck the Roman statesman Cato in a public bath. When the man later apologised, Cato replied that he didn't remember being struck. Seneca admires this: Cato thought it better to ignore the insult than to avenge it.

Seneca argues that a great mind shrugs off small injuries, and that refusing to treat someone as worth revenge is itself the strongest reply. Many people turn small wrongs into big troubles by responding. Like a large animal that ignores yapping dogs, you can choose not to engage.
cards.quote: It is the part of a great mind to despise wrongs done to it
cards.apply_it: Next time someone makes a petty jab, try not responding at all. Notice how quickly it fades.

quiz.question: How did Cato respond when a man who had struck him apologised?
options: He said he didn't remember being struck
quiz.explanation: Cato chose to ignore the insult rather than avenge it.

cards.title: It takes two to fight, so be the first to step back
cards.body:
Seneca's advice for quarrels is practical: answer anger with kindness. A fight needs two people; if only one side keeps it going, it collapses. Even when both are already angry, whoever backs down first is the better person, and the 'winner' of a fight often loses more.

He warns that if you hit back, you give the other person a reason to hit again, and soon you can't get out. Stepping back isn't weakness; it's refusing to be pulled into a cycle you can't control.
cards.quote: If anyone is angry with you, meet his anger by returning benefits for it: a quarrel which is only taken up on one side falls to the ground: it takes two men to fight.
cards.apply_it: In your next tense exchange, respond with one kind or calm sentence instead of a counterattack, and see how the other person reacts.

quiz.question: According to Seneca, who is the better person in a quarrel?
options: The one who wins the argument
The one who gives way first
The one who gets the last word
quiz.explanation: A quarrel needs two sides; whoever steps back first ends it and is the better person.

cards.title: Never make children pay for their parents' quarrels
cards.body:
Among the lessons of the dictator Sulla's cruelty, Seneca says, is this: he drove the sons of his enemies into exile, punishing them for fights they had no part in. Seneca calls it the height of injustice for anyone to inherit a parent's quarrel.

Family feuds, land disputes and political grudges are often passed down for generations, so that young people grow up hating neighbours they have never wronged. Breaking that chain is one of the most valuable things you can do. Judge each person by their own actions.
cards.quote: Nothing is more unjust than that anyone should inherit the quarrels of his father.
cards.apply_it: Is there an old family or community grudge you've inherited? Make one friendly gesture towards someone from 'the other side'.

quiz.question: What did Seneca consider deeply unjust?
options: Treating everyone by their own actions
Making someone inherit their father's quarrels
quiz.explanation: Seneca condemns punishing children for disputes they had nothing to do with.

cards.title: Anger is a weapon you can't pull back once you swing it
cards.body:
Seneca asks: would anyone want to strike so hard that their hand gets stuck in the wound and they lose their balance? That, he says, is what anger is like. We choose light, manageable tools for a reason; anger is heavy, clumsy and impossible to recall once launched.

The strongest actions are the ones we control, like a runner who can slow to a walk when told. Words spoken in rage, a message sent, a door slammed: once out, they can't be taken back, and they often harm you as much as the target.
cards.quote: Does anyone wish to strike his enemy so hard, as to leave his own hand in the wound, and not to be able to recover his balance after the blow? yet such a weapon is anger
cards.apply_it: Before sending an angry message today, ask: 'Can I take this back tomorrow?' If not, wait.

quiz.question: Why does Seneca compare anger to a clumsy weapon?
options: Once used, it can't be recalled and harms the user
It is too light to do any damage
It is the most precise tool we have
It can be put down whenever we like
quiz.explanation: Like a blow that traps your own hand, anger can't be pulled back and throws you off balance.

cards.title: Know your own triggers so you can guard them
cards.body:
Seneca notes that storms give warning signs, and so does anger. People who know a fit is coming take early steps to manage it; we should do the same. He adds that triggers differ from person to person. Some are stung by words, others by actions. One wants respect for their family, another for their looks, their style, or their intelligence.

There's no point guarding against everything equally. Find your own sore spot, the thing that reliably sets you off, and prepare for it in advance.
cards.quote: People do not all take offence in the same way; you ought then to know what your own weak point is, that you may guard it with especial care.
cards.apply_it: Finish this sentence honestly: 'I get angriest when someone…' Decide in advance how you'll respond next time it happens.

quiz.question: Why does Seneca say you should learn your own weak point?
options: So you can hide it from others
So you can guard it with special care
So you can blame others for it
So you can avoid all people
quiz.explanation: Triggers differ between people; knowing yours lets you prepare for it.

cards.title: Tired, hungry people pick fights: look after yourself first
cards.body:
Seneca quotes an old saying that a weary man is quarrelsome, and adds that hunger and thirst have the same effect. When the body is worn down, the mind becomes like a sore spot that hurts at the lightest touch, so even a greeting, a message or a simple question can feel like an attack.

The practical lesson is to notice your physical state before reacting. Many arguments would never happen if people ate, rested or drank some water first. Avoid big conversations when you're exhausted or starving.
cards.quote: it is an old saying that “a weary man is quarrelsome”: and so also is a hungry or a thirsty man
cards.apply_it: Before your next difficult conversation, check yourself: am I hungry, thirsty or tired? If so, fix that first.

quiz.question: Which states does Seneca say make people more quarrelsome?
quiz.explanation: A worn-out body makes the mind irritable, so even small things feel like provocations.

cards.title: Spend time with calm people; tempers are contagious
cards.body:
Seneca says we copy the habits of those we spend time with, much as some illnesses pass by touch. A heavy drinker draws friends into drinking; greed rubs off on those nearby. But good qualities spread too. Living among calm, good-natured people both improves you by example and gives you fewer reasons to lose your temper.

If you struggle with anger, look at your circle. Some people provoke you through pride, others through constant arguing or gossip. Seek out steady, straightforward company.
cards.quote: for our own habits are copied from those with whom we associate, and just as some bodily diseases are communicated by touch, so also the mind transfers its vices to its neighbours.
cards.apply_it: Think of the calmest person you know. Plan to spend more time with them this month.

quiz.question: Why does Seneca advise living with easy-tempered people?
options: Calm people are easier to fool
Angry people are always more honest
It doesn't matter who we live with
We copy the habits of those around us
quiz.explanation: Vices and virtues both spread through company, so calm friends help us stay calm.

cards.title: Act calmer than you feel, and your mind will follow
cards.body:
If you can't stop anger from arising, Seneca says, at least don't let it show. Deliberately make your face more relaxed, your voice softer and your steps slower than usual. Over time, our inner state shifts to match our outward behaviour.

He notes that Socrates spoke more quietly when angry, and his friends could tell. Seneca suggests asking trusted friends to speak frankly to us, especially when we're angry. Calm actions and honest friends are a strong combination.
cards.quote: let us make our countenance more composed than usual, our voice milder, our step slower. Our inward thoughts gradually become influenced by our outward demeanour.
cards.apply_it: When you next feel irritated, deliberately lower your voice and slow your movements for one minute. Notice what happens inside.

quiz.question: What does Seneca suggest doing with your outward behaviour when angry?
options: Make it calmer than usual: milder voice, slower steps
Let it all out to relieve the pressure
Exaggerate it so others back off
quiz.explanation: Seneca believed our inner thoughts gradually follow our outward demeanour.

cards.title: Stop comparing what you got with what others got
cards.body:
Seneca notes that some of our bitterest anger is at friends who gave us less than we expected, or less than they gave someone else. His cure has two parts. If someone else was favoured, enjoy what you have without comparing. If you got less than you hoped, perhaps you hoped for more than was reasonable.

He warns that this resentment can turn even close allies against each other; Julius Caesar, he says, was killed more by friends whose hopes he hadn't satisfied than by enemies. Comparison is a fast road to misery.
cards.quote: A man will never be well off to whom it is a torture to see anyone better off than himself.
cards.apply_it: Notice the next time you compare your share (pay, praise, attention) with someone else's. Instead, name one thing you're glad to have.

quiz.question: What does Seneca suggest if you received less than you hoped?
options: Perhaps you hoped for more than you should have
Compare yourself with those who got more
quiz.explanation: Seneca says to question your expectations rather than resent the giver.

cards.title: Count what you receive as carefully as what you give
cards.body:
Seneca imagines a man who got one honour after another, yet complains about the one he didn't get. His diagnosis: we keep our accounts wrongly. We value what we give highly and what we receive cheaply.

His advice is to thank people for what you received and wait patiently for the rest. If many people are ahead of you, think how many more are behind. Ungrateful book-keeping turns every gift into a grievance; honest book-keeping turns ordinary life into a long list of things to appreciate.
cards.quote: It is, that you keep your accounts wrongly: you set a high value upon what you give, and a low one upon what you receive.
cards.apply_it: Tonight, write down three things someone did for you recently that you haven't properly thanked them for. Thank one of them tomorrow.

quiz.question: What does Seneca call our greatest fault in this passage?
options: Keeping our accounts wrongly: overvaluing what we give
quiz.explanation: We overrate what we give and underrate what we receive, which breeds resentment.

cards.title: Let someone else's anger peak before you try to calm it
cards.body:
Seneca turns to helping other people who are angry. Don't try to argue someone out of the first explosion, he says; at that stage anger is deaf and frantic. Doctors don't treat a swollen eye at its worst, and we shouldn't either. Wait until it starts to ease.

He also warns that scolding an angry person only adds your anger to theirs. Instead, approach gently, distract them, buy time, or show you understand. Calming someone down is a skill of timing as much as words.
cards.quote: You should not attempt to allay the first burst of anger by words: it is deaf and frantic: we must give it scope; our remedies will only be effective when it slackens.
cards.apply_it: When someone near you erupts, say little at first. Listen, stay calm, and only offer a solution once their voice starts to drop.

quiz.question: What is Seneca's advice for the first burst of someone else's anger?
options: Match their anger to show strength
Don't try to argue with it; wait until it eases
quiz.explanation: At its peak anger can't listen; remedies work only once it slackens.

cards.title: We all have faults, so agree to forgive one another
cards.body:
Seneca is blunt: we are all hasty, careless, untrustworthy and ambitious at times. Each of us can find in ourselves the very flaw we blame in others. It is unfair to single out one person for a failing that everyone shares.

From this he draws a gentle conclusion. Since we are imperfect people living among imperfect people, the only path to peace is mutual forgiveness. Even if you haven't wronged this particular person, you have probably wronged someone else, and you are certainly capable of it.
cards.quote: Let us therefore be more gentle one to another: we are bad men, living among bad men: there is only one thing which can afford us peace, and that is to agree to forgive one another.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone you haven't forgiven. Recall one time you needed forgiveness yourself, then decide on one step to let it go.

quiz.question: According to Seneca, what alone can give us peace?
quiz.explanation: Since all of us have faults, mutual forgiveness is the only basis for peace.
